planting.note: Divide and plant established clumps in spring so roots settle before summer heat arrives.

directions: Tuck this dwarf woodland sedge along shaded path edges or beneath taller perennials where its white-margined leaves can be appreciated up close. Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist soil and keep it out of direct afternoon sun, which can scorch the variegated leaf edges. It spreads slowly into a dense, low mat and rarely needs dividing except to propagate more plants. Cut back any tattered winter foliage in early spring before new growth emerges.

planting.note: Set divisions out in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil for fastest establishment.

directions: This fine-textured circumboreal sedge forms soft, pale-green tufts that brighten damp woodland edges and meadow margins. Grow it in moist, fertile soil beneath open canopy or in dappled shade, since it struggles in deep, dry shade. It combines well with ferns and spring ephemerals and needs little care beyond an occasional tidy-up of old foliage. Clumps increase gradually and can be lifted and divided every few years to keep stands vigorous.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring into clay-tolerant, humus-rich soil in shaded sites.

directions: Native to shaded clay woodlands of central Europe, this modest sedge forms a trailing clump of fine evergreen leaves well suited to full or partial shade. It tolerates heavier, clay-based soils better than many ornamental sedges, making it useful where drainage is imperfect. Use it as a groundcover beneath shrubs or trees where little else will establish. Leave the evergreen foliage in place over winter and simply groom out tattered leaves in early spring.

planting.note: Plant into consistently damp, humus-rich soil in spring, ideally near a shaded seep or streambank.

directions: A densely tufted sedge of damp alder and ash woodlands, this species thrives where soil stays reliably moist and light is filtered. Plant it along shaded streambanks, in boggy woodland hollows, or anywhere soggy shade makes other perennials struggle. It forms an upright, arching clump of ribbed green foliage that holds up well through the growing season. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.

planting.note: Install divisions in spring into moist, base-rich woodland soil near seeps or stream margins.

directions: This larger European wood sedge carries wide, gently drooping yellow-green leaves and long, slender fruiting spikes that stand out against darker woodland groundcovers. It favors damp, mineral-rich soils near springs and streamsides, often tolerating deeper shade than many cultivated sedges once established. Site it in moist deciduous woodland plantings where its coarser texture can contrast with ferns and finer sedges. Little maintenance is required beyond dividing crowded clumps every few years.
sources: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland
